utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody and happy new year to all. I hope we all had a good rest and are raring to go. Before we deal with the business of the day, I just wanted to mention that to the best of the Bench's recollection, the only outstanding housekeeping matter is a response from the parties as to whether they will agree to the filing of the maps that were used by Chamber -- by the Chamber on our site visit as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do agree to that being an exhibit. I had understood from my communications with the map unit that perhaps there was going to be a list of the dates of the maps included, but I don't know if that's happened. But in any event, we have no objection to it becoming an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we agree to have the maps admitted into evidence; however, in addition to that we also need to admit into evidence the transcript from the visit and videotapes. They have not been admitted so far, and we suggest that it be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. If that is so, I was under the impression that that had been done. Can I just get confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm advised that, yes, by decision of the Chamber the CDs were -- the electronic full part of it was admitted into evidence and they are already on the e-court, but that the transcript is not yet ready. The Bench will seek guidance here on a procedural point as to how to deal with this point at this point just before the parties present their final arguments. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Obviously, it is important for the transcript to be admitted into evidence so that the parties, when arguing, can refer to it if need be. Mr. Whiting, you are going to stand up on a procedural point, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was just going to suggest that -- that we assign it provisionally a number; and then when it's ready, it just comes into evidence and becoming part of the record. Obviously, since we don't have the transcript, I doubt either side will be able to use it during argument. That's fine with us. We don't need to rely on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then when you say we assign it a number and it comes it forms part of the evidence, you mean we should admit it into evidence in anticipation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It's not a problem to assign a number. The problem is that visiting the site was an official procedural step conducted in the presence of Defence and Prosecution. This is official evidence, and we wonder how is it possible to write a final brief and to have our closing arguments without this being admitted into evidence because this was evidence led at the initiative of the Court. This is a very serious matter. It's not just a matter of assigning a number to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand your objection, Mr. Milovancevic. The electronic record of the visit has been admitted into evidence. I hope you accept that and you understand that. What is outstanding is the -- is a hard copy form, the written form, transcript of that evidence. So it's not as if the evidence is not in -- on the record yet. It is already on the record. It's just the transcribing of it that is not on the record. Does that still make you feel that the step is irregular?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence right now doesn't know when the electronic version was admitted into evidence. It wasn't done until several days ago. It wasn't done until yesterday, and maybe it was done yesterday or today and we are not aware of that. This was an official step of the Bench. When it was a procedural step of the Bench, the Bench went to the site. We had an electronic evidence and we had a transcript, which is a record of that visit. So far, we have not had occasion to see it. Your Honours, it is one thing to watch a videotape depicting the visit, and it is quite a different matter to have a hard copy of a transcript in front of us. It's quite a different manner of working. As it stands now, the Defence needs to produce a transcript for ourselves in order to be able to work on the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand you, Mr. Milovancevic. Are you suggesting that we should therefore -- we cannot proceed with the arguments because of the fact that the transcript of the visit is not there? Is that what you're saying? Which is not a mistake of the Bench, it's just the process it takes to transcribe these documents within registry. Let me just understand what you are saying. Are you saying we cannot proceed with the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not saying that this was a mistake of the Bench, no. I realise that this is a procedure that is time-consuming. However, what is more important is that the registry needs some time in order to complete this, and this is a piece of evidence that the Defence needs, the Prosecution, and the Bench. This is evidence which covers all crime sites. It pertains to the shelling of Zagreb. It is very important in order to assess the systemic and widespread nature of the crime, territorial nexus locations, the prison in Knin, all kinds of matters. I do not want to go through them now because I do not want to waste the time of the Court. To me it seems quite difficult to work under these circumstances. I don't think the Defence can do its work properly, or the Prosecution for that matter, unless this piece of evidence is admitted. This is our position. We simply have to bear in mind the interests of the procedure. Every allegation brought forward by the Prosecution, Your Honours, is directly linked to what we saw when we visited the site, and it can be verified very concretely. The Prosecution did not use that document at all, and this can work to their advantage or that their disadvantage; however, it cannot put the Defence in a disadvantaged position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, what I don't understand, Mr. Milovancevic, is you're saying how can you be able to look at or to judge the bombing of Zagreb and conditions in prisons, and I'm wondering what better way to do so than to look at a movie of it than to read it. Now, what is outstanding, as I'm trying to explain to you, is just the written version of the same report. Now, you are saying - you said a little earlier - that as at yet the electronic version of it had not been admitted into evidence. I can tell you now that by written decision of this Court dated the 28th of November, 2006, this Chamber gave an order that the registrar must provide copies of the five DVD disks and the transcript thereof to the parties. So to suggest that it was not admitted until yesterday, I cannot understand. I do not understand your argument. So the DVDs will be there, and I can't see any better way of seeing what happened on that visit than looking at it on the DVD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours, and I understand what you're saying. I do not deny the fact that you issued such an order on the 28th of November. However, we completed and filed our final brief without seeing these DVDs because they were simply not delivered to us. We did not have them as evidence available to us. We could simply contemplate about them, based on our personal impression, but we were unable to use them, either the DVDs or the transcript, and that's a fact. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a slightly different slant to your problem now. That's an administrative problem. The order was made, as I say, on the 28th of November last year. And as of the day of making that order, I can tell you now that the DVDs were available, because I have -- I have a copy of them in my office. And if you do not have them or you never got them, it's a matter to investigate with registry. But I hear what you say, that if you haven't seen those DVDs, you were put at a disadvantage,. But, you know, I'm not able to answer that question because, as I say, that's within registry. But the order was made early, as ordered. I hear what you say, Mr. Milovancevic, you simply don't have physical possession of the DVDs, and you're saying that made it impossible for you to prepare your final brief. Are you going to add something different?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think you fully understood what I said. It's not that we did not have opportunity, it's that we had to prepare final brief and closing arguments without having seen those DVDs. Another matter is that the Bench gave us maps from the from the site visit, but this was not done by the registry. We asked on a number of occasions. We inquired about these DVDs, and we kept receiving answers,"Yes. They're being prepared. They're being prepared." The last time we inquired was the day before we filed our final briefs. That's what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you haven't told me anything new from what you told me before, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you mentioned -- Mr. Milovancevic, you mentioned the matter of prejudice to the Defence earlier on. As it presently stands, have you prepared submissions that will involve the use of material concerning the site visit, either as contained in the DVD, or otherwise, that is presently before the Trial Chamber? Or do you intend to prepare such material?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- or is it that you're saying, as it presently stands, you're not in a position to make an appropriate assessment because of the fact that the transcript is not yet before the Trial Chamber? Where is the prejudice at this stage? You haven't actually articulated that before the Trial Chamber, and that to me that might be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me first answer the first portion of your question. We did not write down a list of matters to which this visit would pertain and in relation to which facts we would use the transcript, because we were hopeful that we would receive the material every day. We were hoping that we would receive it until the time came for us to file our final briefs. I'm pointing out this problem so that you can understand it. I'm not suggesting at this point in time that the Defence is unable to carry on with our Defence case. We acted in accordance with the order of the Trial Chamber. We produced a final brief to the best of our abilities. We also wrote closing arguments the way we thought that it should be done. All we are doing now is - and we think it is our duty to do so - is to point out to a fault in the procedure. We believe that we need to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So is it that you're saying that your final word should not be closed off until you have had the opportunity to peruse the transcript that comes before the Trial Chamber then? Is that your concern that you would wish to have the opportunity; the transcript coming before the Trial Chamber as it should have done before, that you will now have an opportunity to peruse it, advise yourself, and then make a determination whether you wish to say anything further? Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your question gave rise to a serious dilemma as to how I should answer. I'm saying this because the Defence has a certain position in relation to this piece of evidence led by the Trial Chamber which is linked to all crime bases. Unfortunately, we were not given opportunity. And let us be sure that we understand each other fully because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The question from the Bench by Judge Nosworthy is do you want a second bite at the cherry after the transcript has been placed on record. I think if you can go clearly to that point. We have understood the background of what your problems are. Do you want a second bite at the cherry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since the question by its nature suggests such an opportunity, then, yes, we accept this opportunity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Whiting, you had something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I was going to make the suggestion that perhaps what we could do is proceed with the closing arguments; and then when the transcript becomes available, a date could be set whereby the parties could have a limited - and limited just to that piece of evidence - opportunity to file a written submission on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the Chamber also notes, Mr. Milovancevic, that you did indicate earlier that you are not suggesting that you are unable to proceed with final arguments today. So shall we proceed to that straight away and the Chamber makes the oral order that as and when the transcript is available and has been filed of record, the parties shall be given an opportunity, a very limited opportunity, to file written submissions based strictly on the transcript. And the limitation includes that the parties will be excluded from referring to the DVDs, because the DVDs have been filed some time back and they -- that reference to them should have been -- I am being corrected. That Mr. Milovancevic indicated that he has not received the DVDs. It will be limited to the entire evidence. Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Whiting, please. Your Honours, before my learned friend begins with his closing arguments, I wanted to raise another brief issue and could we please go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, counsel. "There is no evil in doing evil to evil people." Your Honours will recognise these words from this trial. They were written by a Defence witness in this case, Nikola Medakovic, on November 13th, 1991, the day after Serb forces wiped out Saborsko, murdering, expelling, burning, looting as they went. We had lots of back and forth during Mr. Medakovic's testimony about these words. We say that he was trying to justify what had happened the day before in Saborsko, perhaps he claims something else. For the moment, however, I don't want to focus on those particulars, but on how these words provide part of the answer to a question that I am going to guess crossed Your Honours' minds hundreds of times during this trial. That question is: How could this happen? How in the world could this happen? How could people be brought to commit these horrific crimes all over the Krajina; in Dubica, in Saborsko, in Lipovaca, Vukovici, Poljanak, Skabrnja, Nadin, Knin, Bruska? Part of the answer, we say, lies in those ten words: "There is no evil in doing evil to evil people." Many of the people who committed those crimes in the Krajina during 1991, 1992, 1993, all the way to 1995, they had been persuaded that there is no evil in doing evil to evil people. They had been told again and again and again that Croats were Ustashas, that they were threatening, that they were going to destroy the Serbs, to exterminate them, to liquidate them, to commit genocide against them. And I use those highly inflammatory terms because those were the terms used then. Serbs were taught to fear Croats, Croat authorities, and the Croat people alike; and as Milan Babic explained, this fear quickly turned to hatred, a hatred that made it possible for people to expel, to murder, to detain, to torture, to loot, to destroy, to burn. But that's not the whole answer to the question: How did this happen? How in the world could this happen? There is another part of the answer that is implicit in what I have been saying and that is critical to this case, and that is: It could happen. It did happen, because the leaders at the time made it happen. They caused it to happen. They led the people down the path of ethnic hatred, violence, and criminal conduct. These crimes all over the Krajina did not just happen by themselves. People did not on their own just rise up simultaneously and spontaneously to commit these crimes in village after village. No. They were led there. They were brought there by their leaders, and that is what this case is all about. Because in the SAO Krajina, and later in the RSK, the principal leader who brought the people to this point was the accused in this case, Milan Martic. There is no dispute that Milan Martic was the most significant and important Serb leader within the Krajina. Throughout the period in question, he was the military commander within the Krajina, while Milan Babic, who was also important, though who wielded much less power than Milan Martic, was the political leader. From beginning to end, Milan Martic was in charge of the police, which was militarised into a fighting force by early 1991, and he exercised direct command, or significant influence, over the TO. Both Prosecution and Defence witnesses testified about Mr. Martic's stature, influence, and power within the Krajina. Mr. Dobrijevic, for example, a Defence witness, said that Mr. Martic's authority was built very quickly, and he agreed that Mr. Martic had effective and real power in the Krajina. Milan Martic himself spoke many times about his own role and contributions in the Krajina. A few examples. Just after the so-called log revolution in August 1990, that's exhibits 4 and 5 - it's a clip that Your Honours saw many times during the case - Milan Martic told the media to say: "This is the people's police, that this police is protecting this people and is against the Croatian government which does us harm." I'm going to come back to those words later. Just after the events in Plitvice in March of 1991, and this is Exhibit 207, he said: "There is no way we will allow a Croatian Ministry of Internal Affairs police station to be set up at Plitvice. We will wait to see what the army will do; and if they do not resolve the problem, we will drive them all out in a way we will consider to be the most efficient." A few days later, and this is Exhibit 209, Mr. Martic said: "The Knin police force is so busy with the defence of the Krajina borders and the protection of the Serbian people from the Croatian Ministry of Internal Affairs that it simply cannot spend more time solving this type of criminal activity. But it is working on it, and more will be revealed soon." This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What criminal kind of activity was referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This type of criminal activity, Your Honour, was the bombing of a restaurant owned by a Croatian couple. By the way, Your Honours, I'm only going to touch on a few of the statements made by Mr. Martic, but I suggest that it is useful to read them all together because his own words from the time support many of the elements of the case against him. On July 7th, 1991, Martic said -- Mr. Martic said, I'm sorry, and this is Exhibit 213, that: "His men were the only Serbian armed formation in Yugoslavia," and that: "They were well armed and capable of defending the Serbian ethnic areas there." In that same article, Mr. Martic talked about the successes of his units and the modern and heavier equipment that they had acquired. On that same day - it was a significant day because it was a year anniversary of the protest against the Croatian symbols and Croatian police uniforms, so there were a lot of interviews on that day - on that same day Mr. Martic said in another interview, and this is Exhibit 973, that: "Our sole goal is to defend the hearths of our forefathers in Krajina. There is no reason for us to hide anything. We have trained very many men for defence. Lately there are many young women in our ranks." On the 14th of August, 1991, this is Exhibit 626, Mr. Martic spoke of defending not just the SAO Krajina, but also the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and of the mutual assistance and cooperation between these areas. A few days later on the 19th of August, this is Exhibit 215, Mr. Martic said that he never dreamed that he would have such military might at his disposal. Then on September 4th, 1991, Mr. Martic did take his men to Borovo Selo to engage in fighting, called his men Kninija special troops. This is Exhibit 473. In October or November 1991, Mr. Martic said in an interview, it's Exhibit 478: "I can fight against Ustashas. I know how to fight and I have proved it." On the 9th of December, 1991, Mr. Martic spoke at a session of the Presidency of the SFRY. This is Exhibit 917. He spoke against accepting the proposed peace plan and made it clear that he would rather fight than accept the plan. He said: "It seems that the Serbs' eternal fate is to fight until our extinction. If we have to do it, we will do it once more." He said also that: "Until we definitely defeat them, in the military sense, until we force them to capitulate, we are not going to see any fortune." He explained that he could not accept UN forces in: "The territory that we liberated in blood. I'm not saying conquered but liberated, that we have hundreds of casualties who gave their lives for our Krajina." Then on the 12th of December, 1991, Mr. Martic said in Exhibit 518: "The people and police of the SAO Krajina defended with their blood the freedom they had won, and they will continue to do so in the future." About the police, Mr. Martic said that: "They are part of the armed forces and will always be a strong component in coordination with all SO Krajina and Yugoslav forces." So again and again throughout this period, Milan Martic talked about how his men, his men, defended the Krajina. But now, Your Honours, we have an amazing disappearing act. All of a sudden, the police of the Krajina are nowhere to be found. We're told by the Defence, contrary to overwhelming evidence, that really they're nowhere near the major fighting. The police, we are told, did not even exist in Dubica, Bacin, and Cerovljani in September and October 1991. Those men there who everyone thought were the SAO Krajina police, well those were just renegades. In Plaski, near Saborsko, we know that in May of 1991 a special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police was formed at Mr. Martic's suggestion, under the command of Nikola Medakovic. He told us that himself, and he was directly under Mr. Martic's command. But when things got really hot in August and September of 1991, we are told that the special purpose unit was disbanded. When a TO commander in Plaski and the chief of the regular police in Plaski, Bogdan Grba and Dusan Latas, when they referred to special units of the police in documents in November 1991, well, they were just mistaken. In the attack on Saborsko, the police got near Saborsko, but, no, they did not go in. And when Dusan Latas referred in his report to the police going into Saborsko, well, again, he was mistaken. In Skabrnja, the police did not participate in the fighting at all. They were too busy with their regular police duties in Benkovac. The police in Bruska, who in December 1991 wore SAO Krajina police uniforms and announced themselves as the SAO Krajina police, well, they were fakes. The police also had nothing to do with the prisons in Knin, and they were never there. One Defence witness went so far as to claim that the special purpose units of the police did not even exist until 1992. And following this same disappearing act, now we are told that Mr. Martic did not order the attacks on Zagreb in May of 1995, despite his repeated statements that he did just that. Why, Your Honours, is the Defence running from Dubica, from Saborsko, from Skabrnja, from the prisons, from Bruska, from Zagreb? For one simple reason, and that is that the evidence that crimes occurred there is overwhelming. The evidence also proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the SAO Krajina police was involved in each one of those places. In some places, the evidence of police participation is in fact overwhelming. I am going to address each location in turn, even though the Defence in its final brief addressed only some of the crime sites in this case. But, first, let's look at the bigger picture, because Milan Martic is charged in this case with participating in a joint criminal enterprise whose purpose was the forcible removal of Croats from the Krajina in order to create a Serb-dominated state. The Prosecution must prove then, beyond a reasonable doubt, that a group of persons acted together with the common purpose of achieving the criminal end of forcibly removing the Croat population from the Krajina and that Milan Martic participated in the common purpose. With respect to the particular crimes in the indictment, aside from those in Counts 9 and 10, which charge deportation and forcible transfer and which form the core of the common purpose of the JCE, the Prosecution must prove that either they were part of the common purpose of the JCE and were intended by the members of the JCE, including Mr. Martic, to be within the common purpose, or that the crimes were a natural and foreseeable consequence of pursuing the common purpose of forcibly removing the Croat population from the Krajina. Now, let me pause for a moment here to say one thing. I will not talk - you'll be glad to hear - too much in this closing about the legal elements of crimes. But when I do, it will necessarily be in a kind of shorthand and abbreviated way, hopefully accurate, but nonetheless shorthand and abbreviated. And I just want to be sure our complete --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Make sure it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, it's accurate. But our complete and definitive position on the legal elements of the crimes is fully set forth in our brief. Now, under the JCE mode of liability, the Prosecution does not need to prove that Mr. Martic actually committed the crimes or any of the other modes of liability under 7(1), planning, instigating, ordering, or even that men under his command participated in them. Now, the fact is, with the possible exception of the attacks on Lipovaca, Poljanak, and Vukovici, the Prosecution has proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the SAO Krajina police participated and assisted in the attacks in which crimes were committed, at a minimum aiding and abetting in the commission of the crimes, and in some cases that the police even committed crimes. This I will discuss later, when I touch on the specific crime sites charged in this case. But let's stay, for a moment, with JCE, which by the way is not discussed at all in the final brief of the Defence. First, did a plurality of persons work towards a common purpose? Certainly. The evidence establishes that by August of 1991, Serb leaders in the Krajina, in Belgrade, and the JNA were working towards a common goal, even if they had some internal rivalries among themselves at times. Milan Martic himself said this at the time before, during, and afterwards, frequently praising the cooperation that he had with the JNA and the support that he received from Belgrade and from Slobodan Milosevic in particular. Let's just look at one example of such a statement from Mr. Martic. It's from February of 1992, and it's in evidence in this case. I'm going to play it on the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not hearing anything. Does something need to be switched at the desk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, apparently we've got a technical problem. The people in the AV booth can't hear it themselves, so they are trying to solve the problem. Maybe you can come back to it a little later. I know how it affects your argument, your presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I actually have a couple of clips that I was about to play. So I'm wondering maybe if it would not be inconvenient, perhaps we could take the break a little early and then resolve the technical problem and then I could continue if that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you rather we take the break now and come back at half past 10.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Hopefully the technical problem will be resolved during the time. Court is going to adjourn now and reconvene at half past 10.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you proceed, Mr. Whiting, let me just mention that in view of the fact that we took an early break, we will go for one hour, 30 minutes this time and break at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before we broke, I was talking about the evidence that the Serb leaders in the Krajina in Belgrade and within the JNA were working towards a common purpose during 1991. And I spoke about how Mr. Martic himself at the time frequently spoke about the close cooperation that he had with the JNA and the support that he received from Belgrade and from Slobodan Milosevic. And the clip I'm going to play is from Exhibit 951. It's an interview of Mr. Martic from February 1992, so if we can switch over to the Sanction and try and play that clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, the next question is: Was the common purpose of the JCE the forcible removal of Croats from the Krajina? Yes, beyond any doubt. Now, how has this been proven to you? First, witnesses have come in here and have told you that this was the purpose, including Serb witnesses from the Krajina. Milan Babic not only testified that it was the common purpose of the members of the JCE, including Milan Martic, he pled guilty to his own role in the JCE, took responsibility for it, and was sentenced by this Tribunal to 13 years' imprisonment. He admitted that the creation of a Serbian state in the Krajina would include the forcible permanent removal of non-Serb -- of the non-Serb populations from the Serb-dominated areas of Croatia through a discriminatory campaign of persecutions. And I would turn your attention to Exhibit 174, which is his plea agreement and factual basis in the case. In his testimony in this case, he read, and again adopted, a statement that he made when he pled guilty before this Tribunal, and I'm going to play that for you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "Q. Mr. Babic, could you read the statement, please? "A. I said the following. 'Thank you, Your Honour. I come before this Tribunal with a deep sense of shame and remorse. I have allowed myself to take part in the worst kind of persecution of people simply because they were Croats and not Serbs. Innocent people were persecuted. Innocent people were evicted forcibly from their houses, and innocent people were killed. Even I learned what had happened -- even after I had learned what had happened, I kept silent. Even worse I continued in my office and I became personally responsible for the inhumane treatment of innocent people. 'The regret that I feel is the pain that I have to live with for the rest of my life. These crimes and my participation therein can never be justified. I'm speechless when I have to express the depth of my remorse for what I have done, and the effect of my sins and the effect they have had on the others. I can only hope that by expressing the truth, by admitting to my guilt and expressing the remorse, can serve as an example for those who still mistakenly believe that such inhumane acts can ever be justified. 'Only truth can give the opportunity to the Serbian people to relieve themselves of its -- their collective burden of guilt. Only this, an admission of guilt on their part, makes it possible for me to take responsibility for all the wrongdoings that I have done. I hope that the remorse that I have expressed will make it easier for others to bear their pain and suffering. I have come to understand that enmity and division can never make it easier for us to live together. I have come to understand that the fact that we all belong to the same human race and that it is more important than any difference and I have come to understand that only through friendship and confidence can we live together in peace and friendship and thus make it possible for our children to live together in a better world. 'I have asked help from God to make it easier for me to repent and I am thankful to God for making it possible to help me express my repentance. I ask my brothers, Croats, to forgive us, their brothers Serbs, and I pray for the Serb people to turn to the future and to achieve the kind of compassion that will make it possible to forgive the crimes. And, lastly, I place myself at the full disposal of this Tribunal and the international justice. Thank you very much.' "Those were my words then, and I stand by them even today."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you -- are you able to refer the Bench to any corroborating evidence of that position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm just about to. It's also set forth in the brief, but I'll also refer to some of the corroboration in this case. Witness MM-079 testified that Mr. Martic told him in 1991 that: "The Serbs of Krajina wanted to live in one single country with all the other Serbs from Yugoslavia, including Serbia." To live with the Serbs, he said. MM-03 testified that Mr. Martic and the army had the same goal, to link up Serb lands and cleanse the area of Croats. He said that this meant that Croats would no longer be living there. MM-078 testified that there was: "Constant pressure on the Croatian citizens of Knin," starting as early as 1990. Look also at the statements of Mr. Martic at the time. And before I do that, I would note, going back to Mr. Babic, that in our view also he was cross-examined on the goals of the joint criminal enterprise and the larger issues; and, therefore, we think, even if there was no corroboration, it could be relied upon by this Trial Chamber. However, the corroboration is overwhelming, both in terms of testimony and the events on the ground that actually occurred, which I will touch on in a moment. Look at the statements of Mr. Martic at the time. Remember that statement that he made to the media in August of 1990. It's Exhibits 4 and 5 that I referred to earlier, and I said I would come back to. It's a videotape that you've seen of him many times of him standing by a truck and saying this is the people's police. Remember what he says, he says the people's police: "Is protecting this people and is against the Croatian government which does us harm." Who is referring to when he says "this people"? That the police is protecting "this people" from the Croatian government? Is he referring to all of the people of the Krajina, regardless of ethnicity? No. No, he's referring to the Serbs in the Krajina. On July 7th, 1991, Mr. Martic said: "The Krajina police are defending Serbian land and the Serbs' ethnic area." That's Exhibit 498. On that same day he said that his men and the JNA had the same goals, to defend a people who had expressed its will at a referendum on the 12th of May, 1991; that it wanted to join Serbia, Montenegro, and others who want to live in Yugoslavia. That's Exhibit 973. Again, which people are we talking about here? Serbs, of course. These repeated statements were not just statements made in the heat of the moment. Years later, in October of 1994, Mr. Martic still used the same language, stating in an interview that is Exhibit 496 that: "I thought we had to liberate our ethnic territories." Now, in July and August and into the fall of 1991, at the very same time that Mr. Martic was saying that the role -- that the job of the Krajina police was to defend Serbs, Serb lands, Serb ethnic areas, he was issuing ultimatums demanding that the Croatian police leave Croat villages in the Krajina. So was there really a place for Croats in this new Serbian state that was being created? No, clearly not. The state was for Serbs. The police was going to defend Serb areas, defend Serbs. Croats had no place there. But even more than from the testimony of witnesses in this case and the statements made at the time, including those by Mr. Martic, we know what the common purpose was of the joint criminal enterprise from what actually happened in the Krajina. What happened in Croat village after Croat village after Croat village screams out louder than any witness could. Again and again and again, Croat villages were isolated by barricades, shelled, provoked, and then attacked in a manner that was designed to drive out the Croat population. The evidence of this pattern is compelling. It happened before the intense fighting of the fall of 1991, during that fighting, and after that fighting. It happened in Potkonje, Lovinac, Glina, Struga, Kijevo, Vrlika, Drnis, Dubica, Bacin, Cerovljani, Saborsko, Poljanak, Vukovici, Lipovaca, Skabrnja, Nadin, Bruska, and other places. After the RSK was formed at the beginning of 1992, it continued to happen, with the participation and sanction of the police in places like Kijevo and Knin, until by 1994 nearly all of the Croats were driven out of the RSK. It can be presumed that one intends the natural consequences of one's actions, particularly when these consequences occur again and again and again. I'm not going to go through every village, every instance. It is set out in detail in our final brief. I do, however, want to focus for a few moments on the first example that we point to, Potkonje, because it says a lot about the pattern that was to follow. The attack occurred there on the 2nd of May, 1991. Although the SAO Krajina police was not doing anything at the time about Serbs who were arming themselves in the SAO Krajina and was even participating in that arming, it targeted Potkonje, which was at least 95 percent Croat, for an operation to seize weapons there. It could not have been missed by anybody that this would send a clear message to the Croat population. They would be disarmed while neighbouring Serb villages would remain armed. Witness MM-78 testified that the police "wreaked havoc" during the operation, and that the psychological effects on the Croat population were "devastating," and that it caused the Croat population, quite predictably, to leave. On cross-examination, this witness, Prosecution witness MM-78, testified that what happened in Potkonje was in line with the policy of the Krajina authorities at the time to expel Croats from their homes and villages which would occur thereafter in all areas where Croats lived. He said that what happened "was only to confirm what was going to happen later. Potkonje, Kijevo, Vrpolje, all the places where Croats were in absolute majority or a significant majority, disappeared." That's at transcript 4521 to 22. Now, a Defence witness, MM-96, also testified about Potkonje and about the police operation there. He testified that during the operation, yes, the police fired their weapons in the air, searched houses, arrested several inhabitants, and took them to the prison in Knin. He confirmed what MM-78 said, that the operation had a devastating psychological impact on the Croat population and that it caused Croats to leave. He also made an important concession during the cross-examination about the nature of the Potkonje operation. The clip that I'm going to play for you is from page 7067 of the transcript, and because the English is a little bit hard to hear, I've asked that the transcript also be played at the same time while the tape is being played.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "Q. I want to turn now to what happened in Potkonje. You would agree with me, would you not, that the population of Potkonje in 1991 was 95 percent Croat and about 5 percent Serb? "A. Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not familiar with the exact information. One thing that is certain is Potkonje was a predominantly Croat village. I'm not sure about the exact percentages, but there were a good deal more Croats. That much is certain. "Q. I understand you may not know the exact percentage, but that percentage, when you say 'predominantly Croat,' would you agree that it's almost completely Croat; that is, over 90 percent Croat? "A. I would tend to agree, yes. "Q. Now, you testified that you never received an order 'that involved making a difference between citizens based on their ethnic, political, religious, or any other affiliation.' Do you remember that testimony? "A. I do. And I still believe that my behaviour conformed with that. "Q. But then just a few minutes after you said that, and actually it appears on the next page in the transcript at 6847, you testified that you received an order to disarm the Croats in Potkonje who had armed themselves. Wasn't that an order directed at an ethnic group, the Croats? "A. If you look at that particular operation, I suppose you could say that this was the case."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the concession that this Defence witness makes here is significant for two reasons. First, it confirms that from the very beginning, from May 1991, Croats were singled out and targeted by the police. And they were targeted in a way that would obviously cause them to have fear and to leave. Second, even though the witness originally testified that he had never received an order that involved making a distinction between citizens based on ethnic affiliation, he admitted that in fact the order to conduct the operation in Potkonje was directed at an ethnic group, the Croats. For that moment in the questioning, we submit, the official line, the justifications, the excuses, the rationalizations, the double-speak fell away, and the truth about what happened in Potkonje emerged. And Potkonje was just the beginning. The later attacks were of course even more fierce and more devastating. Mr. Van Lynden was told in July of 1991 by Serb soldiers, after the attack on Struga, that their aim was to rid the region of Croats, and he described himself how this -- he saw this as an early attempt at ethnic cleansing. And that is exactly what happened in all of the Croat areas of the Krajina after that. In light of all of the evidence taken together, the witness testimony, the statements at the time, the documents, and, most importantly perhaps, what actually happened on the ground, there can be no doubt about the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. It was to target Croat areas and to force Croats to leave by whatever means necessary, including widespread crimes. Not only was that the purpose of the JCE, that is in fact what happened in the Krajina during the years charged in this indictment. So how did Mr. Milan Martic participate in this joint criminal enterprise? Remember, first, the ways that Milan Babic admitted to participating in the JCE, which were found by the Trial Chamber in his case to be sufficient to enter a finding of guilt and to sentence him to a period of 13 years' imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I at this stage, Mr. Whiting, before you go any further pose a question to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is this Trial Chamber at liberty to refer to and use any finding of another Trial Chamber touching and concerning the guilt of Babic and his participation, if any, in the joint criminal enterprise; and if yes, please tell me why. We do not know the evidence that went before that Trial Chamber, whether it is similar to or different from the evidence before us. I would like you to take me through the paces of that one. What Babic said before this Court and adopted, I would make a distinction in that case because that is very real evidence before us. However, now, when it comes to the finding of another Trial Chamber under circumstances where he's pleaded guilty, how does it import on this Trial Chamber in adopting it for use in reaching a finding against Milan Babic in this indictment -- sorry, case against Mr. Martic in this indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do believe that this Court can rely upon the findings because the material that was before the Trial Chamber in Milan Babic's case has been placed before this Trial Chamber and is in evidence. The factual basis for the plea is in evidence as Exhibit 174. So the facts are before the Trial Chamber, and of course in our submission they conform with the facts as were testified to by the witness. In addition, the decision of the Trial Chamber is before the -- is put in -- placed into evidence, and the Trial Chamber can see from that decision what facts were relied upon by the Trial Chamber in reaching its findings. I would say, therefore, that this Trial Chamber could make both evidentiary and legal use of these findings. Evidentiary use because these facts were what Mr. Babic admitted to, what he confirmed, what he said he did; and therefore -- and they've been put into evidence and confirmed by the witness. And, therefore, it can be relied upon as an evidentiary matter. It can also -- that is in terms of what he says he did and what he says the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise was. And now, let me just be clear. I'm not suggesting for a moment that the Trial Chamber is bound by the findings, merely that it may rely upon them safely. Secondly, I think the Trial Chamber can rely upon them as a legal matter because the Trial Chamber in Mr. Babic's case made certain factual findings. These are the ways that Mr. Babic participated in the joint criminal enterprise according to his admission, and then made a legal finding that these ways were sufficient to enter a finding of guilt to participating in the joint criminal enterprise and committing the crime of persecutions. And that legal analysis can be relied upon by this Trial Chamber. For example -- at least for guidance if the Trial Chamber makes certain findings, factual findings, about how Mr. Martic participated in the joint criminal enterprise could be guided on the issue of whether that would be sufficient to enter a finding of guilt with the joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The problem, as I said, is really the admission by Mr. Babic and the finding of guilt by that Trial Chamber. I do not think that it can import on this Trial Chamber's decision. But what I've extracted is that that aside the actual statements of fact and the adoption and the findings could be considered and could be used, but thank you for your submissions, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope they were helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: They are very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Should I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to -- is it so that what Mr. Babic said happened in his case, did he testify about that being the manner of participation or something -- some similar action being the manner of participation by Mr. Milan Martic in this trial? Did he testify about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, he testified about how he participated, and then he testified about the things that Mr. Martic did. Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That answered my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, I would -- when in considering in whatever manner that you choose to do, Mr. Babic's testimony and his guilty plea and the factual basis for his guilty plea, I would turn your attention again to Exhibit 174, which is his guilty plea and the factual basis that he admitted to. And in paragraph 33 of the factual basis, it sets out the various ways that Milan Babic admitted to participating in the joint criminal enterprise. I will not go through all of them. You'll have an opportunity to look at it. But can there really be any doubt based on the evidence that has been presented in this case that Milan Martic's participation in the JCE far exceeded anything that Milan Babic did? Can there be any doubt that Milan Martic held more power, more influence, had stronger support from Mr. Milosevic in Belgrade? That he was the highest and most important military commander within the Krajina? And these were, after all, military operations that we're talking about. Now, we say that Milan Martic participated in the JCE in a myriad of ways. I will not list them all here, but they include: Commanding military structures in the Krajina, including the police, which Mr. Martic militarised during 1991; organising the military training of police and volunteers at Golubic; obtaining funding and arms from Belgrade for the police and for the Serbs of the Krajina; creating special purpose units that participated in military operations; provoking conflict with Croat villages and making demands and ultimatums upon them; allowing police forces under his command to participate, along with the JNA and TO forces, in military attacks on Croat villages with the purpose of devastating those villages and driving out the Croat population; encouraging the JNA and political leaders in Belgrade to support the Serbs in their conflict in the Krajina; ensuring close cooperation among Serb forces during the conflict in the Krajina; maintaining close cooperation and coordination among members of the joint criminal enterprise; supporting separate government structures within the Krajina that supported the purpose of the JCE, in part through his various positions that he held in the Krajina governments; engaging in inflammatory and well-publicised rhetoric that caused Serbs to fear Croats and to make them believe that they could be safe only in a state of their own, free of Croats, and made it clear to Croats that the Krajina was not safe for them. It's clear that Mr. Martic did not simply participate in the joint criminal enterprise, he was an essential component to its success. Now, before talking about the particular crimes that either fell within the joint criminal enterprise or were a foreseeable consequence of pursuing the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, let me just pause for a moment to comment on this mode of liability, this joint criminal enterprise. It is an essential and well-established mode of criminal responsibility at this Tribunal, having been repeatedly affirmed in many cases, most recently in the Krajisnik case. As we said in our opening address in this trial, this mode of liability is a recognition of the fact that these kinds of crimes are rarely accomplished by one person acting alone or even by a single entity. Rather, they can only be accomplished by various entities working together towards a common goal. Let's now talk specifically about the various crime sites charged in the indictment. The crimes committed in Dubica, Bacin, Cerovljani, Saborsko, Poljanak, Vukovici, Skabrnja, Nadin, and Bruska, and Knin in 1991, and the crimes committed against Croat civilians all over the RSK during the years 1992 through 1995, were all within the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. In each of these locations, aside from Knin which is just about the detentions, overwhelming force was used and widespread crimes were committed, including murder, looting, and destruction. One purpose of the attack and the purpose of the crimes was to drive out the Croats. In the alternative, the crimes committed in these villages were plainly a foreseeable consequence of the pursuit of the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise to forcibly remove Croats from the Krajina. They were foreseeable in two ways. First, they were simply a foreseeable consequence of such a purpose. It could be expected that if there were a common purpose to forcibly remove Croats, pursued by the highest military and political authorities in the Krajina and in Belgrade, through a process of demonising the Croat side and causing fear and hatred among Serbs, then it would invite serious crimes against Croat persons and their property. It would be open season on Croats. They did not enjoy the protection of the government or the police. The police was there, remember, to defend Serb lands, Serb ethnic areas, Serb people. The crimes were also foreseeable because of the pattern of what happened before. Remember that by the crime crimes occurred in Dubica and Saborsko and Skabrnja in October and November of 1991, there had already been a well-established pattern of attacks where it could be seen that such crimes would occur as a part of these attacks in Struga, in Kijevo, Vrlika, Drnis. As a result, by October of 1991, everyone, including Milan Martic, was on notice that such crimes would occur, but the attacks continued on in the same manner, if anything becoming even stronger and more aggressive. Although, in some instances, there were skirmishes back and forth between Serbs and Croats before Serb forces attacked a village, such as in Saborsko and in Skabrnja, this cannot be a justification for the attacks that occurred later. First, the evidence is that these villages were under siege and were provoked by superior Serb forces long before any full-scale attack occurred. Mr. Babic testified about the pattern that occurred after August 1991, and witnesses in these villages confirmed this pattern. Serb forces provoked conflict with Croat areas, the Croat side responded, and then Serb forces attacked with overwhelming force and committed crimes, including murder, expulsion, looting, and torching. This is at 1572 to 1574 of Mr. Babic's testimony. It cannot be that simply because Croat defenders in these villages at times fought back, at times responded to provocations, that then the door was wide open to an attack that was plainly designed to wipe out the village. Second, the scale and nature of the attacks show that another objective was afoot. These attacks were not simply designed to achieve a military objective; rather, the size of the attacks and the widespread crimes committed during these attacks show what was really going on behind the justifications, the rationales, the double-speak. The Serb forces wanted to get rid of Croat villages within the Krajina, and that is what they did. Now, let's look at Dubica, Bacin, and Cerovljani. The evidence establishes that more than a month after these areas fell to Serb forces, on October 22nd -- they fell around September 13th, 1991. And more than a month later, on October 22nd, 1991, some 56 civilians, nearly all of them Croat, nearly all of them elderly, were massacred, executed. The evidence also shows that both during the take-over of this area in September 1991 and afterwards, other civilians were murdered. And I would point the Court in particular to the evidence of Antun Blazevic and Ana Kesic, Exhibits 273 and 258, regarding these additional murders. There was no military justification whatsoever for these murders or for the looting and destruction that occurred in these Croat villages. Did the SAO Krajina police participate in the October massacre in Dubica and Bacin? We say the evidence says yes, beyond a reasonable doubt. The Defence concedes in paragraph 52 of their brief that the evidence shows that members of Velja Radjunovic's group participated in the massacre. So the only question really is: Was Radjunovic's group the police of the SAO Krajina? Again, the answer is yes. First, let's recall the circumstances in Dubica at the time, and if we could switch to the Sanction I'll show a map. Your Honours will recognise that it's your map, just a portion of it. Serb forces took Dubica and Bacin, as I said, and Cerovljani in mid-September 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to enlarge the map a little bit to occupy the entire screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not sure we are ready to do that, Your Honour. You caught us -- the point I'm going to make is going to be kind of visible from this I think. There we go. Okay. Thank you. As I said, Serb forces took Dubica and Bacin and Cerovljani in mid-September of 1991, just one or two days after they took Kostajnica, which you can see on the map there and which is approximately 20 kilometres away. Now, Mr. Martic's police, the evidence shows, were also present at this time in Glina and in Dvor, which are not visible now on the zoomed-in map but are visible on the other map. I think Glina is just at the very top there. It's just been cut off a little bit, and Dvor is just north of Bosanski Novi. All of these villages are in the area which was referred to as Banija. Capturing Kostajnica and Dubica and Bacin and Cerovljani in mid-September 1991 were significant military victories for the SAO Krajina and Serb forces, particularly since they established important connection points with Serb areas in Bosnia right across the river. And there can be no doubt about Mr. Martic's involvement and interest. On July 23rd of 1991, Mr. Martic met with the commanders in Banija, including the commander of the war staff in Kostajnica. And Captain Dragan assessed that: "Unity had been established in the conduct of all operations in this area." That's Exhibit 582 and it's referring to Banija. Some time in August or September, before the attack on Kostajnica, Mr. Martic stated in a press conference that "Kostajnica will fall again because the MUP forces," meaning the Croatian MUP forces, "have no food, water, or electricity, and they are surrounded on all sides by the fighters from Banija." That's Exhibit 479. We know that after Kostajnica fell in mid-September 1991, Stevan Borojevic led a special police unit there and that was subordinated to Mr. Martic. But the Defence would now have you believe that from mid-September 1991, when these areas came under Serb control, until October 21st of 1991, and even after, Mr. Martic and the JNA and the TO allowed Dubica and Bacin to be controlled by a rogue police unit, even though these locations are just 20 kilometres from Kostajnica and were extremely important strategically. They were close to Bosnia, close to the front line, and close to the JNA base in Zivaja. But the evidence from Defence witnesses, and it is cited in footnote 389 of our final brief, is that the police and the JNA did not tolerate rogue units, and so it is impossible to believe that they would tolerate this for such a long period of time in such an important location. Moreover, the witnesses who testified at the trial and who were actually in Dubica and Bacin at the time say that Radjunovic's police were the SAO Krajina police. MM-22 testified repeatedly, both in direct examination and in cross-examination, that there was just one police in town, that police led by Radjunovic, and that it was the SAO Krajina police; that this was written on their uniforms and vehicles and that they had their headquarters in town, in Dubica, in the centre of Dubica. This evidence was corroborated by the evidence of Josip Josipovic. Now, the Defence cites an unsigned Official Note of an interview with Mr. Josipovic in paragraph 50 of their brief, but they edit the quotation in a way to make it read a certain way. Go back and look at what it says. In fact, we say the quotation is completely unclear and in any event was never adopted by the witness who provided clear testimony on the issue in court. A truck marked SAO Krajina police was used to bring people to the fire station on the 21st of October, 1991, and Ana Kesic testified that she was brought there by Velja Radunovic himself. And if Radunovic's unit was really a rogue unit, why didn't anything happen to them after the massacre? Why weren't they arrested and prosecuted for what they had done? We know that the police knew what was going on. Look at MM-22's evidence about his encounters with the police shortly after the massacre, and certainly the JNA and TO know what happened, but nothing happened to Radunovic's unit. Mr. Martic only disbanded the unit a month later and only because they got into a kind of political dispute about annexing themselves to Bosnia. And even then the evidence is Radunovic's men were simply sent to the front line and sometime later they were back again. No, Your Honours, they were not a rogue unit, they were the SAO Krajina police, just as the witnesses said they were. Let's turn now to Saborsko. Saborsko's not dealt with at all by the Defence in their final brief, and it is discussed extensively in our brief, so I will not talk long about it. But there can be no doubt that the regular police of the SAO Krajina, under Dusan Latas, the special police unit under Nikola Medakovic, and the state security or DB under in Plaski under Djuro Ogrizovic, all of which were within the Ministry of the Interior and subordinated to Mr. Martic participated in the attack on Saborsko. MM-37 confirmed this in his evidence, and it is confirmed by numerous documents, including attack orders and reports written after the attack by Mr. Latas and Mr. Ogrizovic. The only witness who tried to minimise the role of the police in Saborsko, even though even he conceded that the police participated, was Defence witness Medakovic. We would submit, however, that the evidence of this witness was wholly incredible on key points. He claimed that the special police units no longer existed in November of 1991 but could not really explain references to them in documents. He claimed not to know anything about a DB unit in Plaski, despite references to such a unit in documents. He claimed that the police did not enter Saborsko, despite clear evidence to the contrary. And remember his perspective on the events, as reflected both in the letter that he wrote the day after the attack on Saborsko, that's Exhibit 269, and in this courtroom, where he claimed, and it's at page 9247 of the transcript, that the Croatian side deliberately caused the murders of civilians in Saborsko in order to gain the pity of Europe. Skabrnja. The evidence establishes beyond any possible doubt that the Benkovac police under Bosko Drazic participated in the attack on Skabrnja, as did the Territorial Defence, the TO. The evidence also shows that there was no military justification for the attack on Skabrnja and Nadin, and certainly no justification for the type of attack that occurred. The Defence picks out parts of Marko Miljanic's testimony to suggest that in Skabrnja there were well-armed and well-manned Croatian forces that had taken JNA officers prisoner. In fact, while Mr. Miljanic did say that there was a defensive force in Skabrnja, and he told Your Honours about it, he said that they had minimal weapons. He described them, and they only held JNA officers who came to their area, and then only briefly. Moreover, he said that after The Hague truce was signed on November 5th, 1991, there were no provocations, and he said that he was warned by a JNA captain that they were done for and that Ratko Mladic was going to defeat them. He said that they had identified basements as shelters in Skabrnja in case of attack, and Your Honours know the importance of those basements in Skabrnja and what happened there during the attack. He said also that the attack began with artillery fire on the village and that during the attack civilians were taken out of basements and killed. Now, in their final brief, the Defence simply presents Zoran Lakic's version of what happened in Skabrnja and virtually ignores, or rather, ignores virtually all the other evidence. But did Mr. Lakic's evidence hold up in court? Let's take a moment to look at some of the key points of his testimony. First of all, he testified that the TO did not participate in the attack on Skabrnja. On direct examination he said that he entered Skabrnja only after the action ceased. And on cross-examination he re-affirmed that except for the medical unit that went in later, "not a single unit of mine was o there on that date, the 18th of November." But that's clearly not true. The very next Defence witness, Nada Pupovac, testified as follows, this is at 10399. "Q. Isn't it true that on the 18th of November, 1991, members of the Territorial Defence participated in the fighting? "A. They did take part, under the command of the JNA." Moreover, numerous exhibits about the attack and about crimes committed in Skabrnja all confirm that the TO participated. The Defence tries to gloss over this issue in paragraph 17 of their brief by saying that: "There is conflicting evidence about whether the TO participated in the action itself." But this is not a minor detail. Whether the TO -- Mr. Lakic was the commander of the TO and whether the TO participated in the attack or not is a core issue, and it cannot be something that Mr. Lakic was mistaken about. Second, Mr. Lakic testified that the JNA went to Skabrnja on November 18th to try to reach a peaceful solution and that their intent was not to attack. Along these lines, both he and the next witness, Ms. Pupovac, claimed that Lieutenant Stefanovic was essentially ambushed when he was speaking on the megaphone, but these claims are plainly untrue. MM-80 testified that he learned Skabrnja was going to be attacked the night before, on November 17th. And Exhibit 107, a very important exhibit, the notes of the commander of the operation, Momcilo Bugunovic, confirm that on November 17, the day before, preparations were being made to "mop-up Skabrnja and Nadin." Now, whatever the term "mop-up" means in this context certainly did not mean going to make peace. These notes also show that Lieutenant Stefanovic was not killed because he was ambushed but because he was "stubborn and went first." Now, the Defence also tries to minimise the importance of Exhibit 107, an exhibit by the way that the Defence put into evidence. In footnote 31 of their brief, because they say that the notes are handwritten and because they claim that say they "often lack precision and consistency," but they point to no examples to support this characterisation of theirs. But really just the opposite is true, Your Honours. The notes in Exhibit 107 are so significant because they are not packaged in an official report with excuses and rationalizations and editing, but rather they represent raw, unfiltered notes from the time. Finally, with respect to the reason behind the attack on Skabrnja, Mr. Lakic conceded finally in cross-examination, it's at 10227, that he did not know the reason behind the attack. Third, Mr. Lakic testified, as did Ms. Pupovac after him, that the police did not participate in the attack on Skabrnja. Mr. Lakic claimed that the police stayed in Benkovac and did their regular policing duties there, also plainly untrue. Exhibit 107 establishes, without any doubt, that the police participated in the attack. There are numerous references in the document to problems of coordination among the various participants, including the TO, the police. And Bosko Drazic, himself, was present at a meeting two days after the attack, on the 20th of November, 1991, to review what occurred in Skabrnja. He's recorded as having said at that meeting that there was "very good planning," and that "the operation showed positive results and very much so!" Moreover, reports about crimes committed in Skabrnja show that Drazic himself was present during the attack. Fourth, Mr. Lakic initially claimed that the only thing that he knew about civilians killed in the attack was that some had been killed during shelling and that a corpse was uncovered sometimes after the operation. That's at 10181 of the transcript. But as the witness was countered with document after document showing that the crimes in Skabrnja were widespread and immediately known, this answer evolved. At pages 10266 to 10267, he said that in fact he knew that there had been many victims two or three days after the action, and that certain officers wanted to "shift the blame" to a third party. When he was shown Exhibit 107 and the notes of the meeting that he also attended on November 20th, 1991, at which crimes were discussed, he said that "the information to the effect that there was killing and that there were victims reached us quite soon." That's at 10280. Then at 10285 to 10286, he admitted that he knew just two days after the attack on Skabrnja that there had been "crimes, robberies, and barbarities in Skabrnja." Finally, with respect to these two Defence witnesses, Mr. Lakic and Ms. Pupovac, it must be noted that despite their sweeping claims, and what motivated these claims you might ask, about what happened or didn't happen during the Skabrnja operation, both of them according to their own testimony had extremely limited perspectives on what happened there and could not know everything that was happening in Skabrnja. At the end of the day, neither the testimony of Mr. Lakic nor of Ms. Pupovac refutes the overwhelming testimony that the SAO Krajina police participated in the attack, along with the TO and the JNA, and that numerous and widespread crimes were committed during that attack. Bruska. The evidence that this crime was committed by members of the SAO Krajina police is of course overwhelming. The attackers repeatedly identified themselves as being the Krajina police, Martic's men, and they wore uniforms which said Milicija Krajina or Krajina police on them. Moreover, when Ante Marinovic was recovering in the hospital from his injuries, a man wearing a Milicija uniform came into his room and said: "This Ustasha should be slaughtered immediately." In the case of this evidence, the only response offered by the Defence, and perhaps it's possibly the only response, that the men were not really SAO Krajina police, but were simply pretending, were fakes. This theory, however, is not supported by any evidence and is really just pure speculation. It certainly does not amount to reasonable doubt. Moreover, given the late date that we're talking about, this is December 20th, 1991, after all, given the location of Bruska, which is located roughly between Benkovac and Knin, given the evidence that the SAO Krajina police did not tolerate renegades, it is impossible to believe that these attackers at Bruska were not in fact the SAO Krajina police. In addition, Exhibits 286 and 919 show that on November 20th, 1991, a month before the murders in Bruska, the SAO Krajina police arrested Croats from Medvidja and detained them until they were exchanged in June of 1992. Now, Medvidja is a predominantly Serb village which is near Bruska. And in fact, Ante Marinovic testified that before the events on the 20th of December, 1991, men who identified themselves as Martic's police came from Medvidja to Bruska and harassed the population of Bruska. If the SAO Krajina police is indisputably making arrests and detaining Croats in this area of Medvidja in November of 1991, it is impossible to imagine that there is some rogue unit calling themselves the SAO Krajina police in nearby Bruska. They're not from Bruska, they come to Bruska one month later, in December of 1991. No, the evidence shows that the men who committed these murders in Bruska, they were SAO Krajina police. Finally, the Defence claims that the police conducted a professional investigation after these murders, but Exhibit 404 says otherwise and suggests that the police knew who had committed the murders and were covering it up. Let's move on to the crimes committed in the prisons. The Defence does not discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go to the prisons, what does Exhibit 404 say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Exhibit 404 is a report from a JNA security organ person. I'm not exactly sure which one, but I think I do -- but I think I know and that can be checked. And it says according to information received from a reliable source, the police in Benkovac -- I believe in Benkovac know who committed the murders in Bruska, and a that person who knew specifically had been transferred out to another place. And the implication or the suggestion is that this was done in order to cover it up and hide who had actually committed the murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just before you go on. If the acts in issue at the different locations had in fact been committed by a rogue group, would that change the position, and what would your answer be? Suppose there were in fact such a finding by the Trial Chamber, as unlikely as you consider it to be. If you can't answer that question at this stage, maybe you could defer it to a later stage. But I would like you to think about it and respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can answer it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, because I'm interested to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, the question would be -- well, in our view it would fall within the scope of the joint criminal enterprise, either within the -- what's called JCE 1; that is, that these crimes were within the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, or JCE 3, which is that they were a foreseeable consequence of pursuing the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. It would have to be found that these crimes were -- fell into one of those categories. So in other words, as I said earlier in the -- in my closing, the Trial Chamber does not need to find that men under Mr. Martic participated in all of these locations. It would only need -- it can make that finding or not make that finding. If that finding is not made with respect to a particular location, then the question becomes if there is a finding of a joint criminal enterprise and Mr. Martic's participation, whether that crime fell within the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise or was a foreseeable consequence of it. So, I suppose the -- it's a long way of saying that a -- a finding by the Trial Chamber that it was committed by a rogue unit would not necessarily mean that there was no criminal liability for Mr. Martic for that -- the crimes committed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, if we could move to the prisons. The Defence does not discuss the crimes at the prisons at all in their final brief. And we have discussed it in our submission, so I will touch on this only briefly. It is plain that the position of the Defence is that the police had nothing to do with the prison in Knin. The evidence, however, shows otherwise. The prison was run by Stevo Plejo, who was recruited into the police by Milan Martic and was trained at Golubic. He became warden of the prison in Knin in August of 1991, even though he had no experience and there were other guards there who had significantly more experience with prisons than he did and even though he claimed himself he didn't want the job. It seems there can be only one conclusion that why he got that job and that was because of his affiliation with Mr. Martic. Prisoners were brought to the prison by the police, there's no dispute about that, prisoners of war, and they were released from the prison under direction of the police. Mr. Plejo himself admitted - and I think this was from -- this was during questioning from the Trial Chamber, and it's at 8921 - that the police had a role in running the prison all the way until at least mid-November of 1991. In light of these facts, the testimony of the victims that the SAO Krajina -- that members of the SAO Krajina police came to the prison and beat and tortured prisoners there is entirely credible. Moreover, the detentions and the beatings in the prison were in furtherance of the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. Exhibits 286 and 919 show that prisoners were detained from Glina, Plaski, Lovinac, Vrlika, Kijevo, Drnis, and Skabrnja, and detained as a result of the attacks on those villages. In other words, as part of those attacks, those prisoners were detained and brought to Knin. The evidence also shows that detentions and beatings of Croats were a way to cause further fear among the Croat population, to further intimidate them, and to cause them to leave. The Defence also does not touch at all on the evidence of continued crimes against Croats during the years 1992 to 1995. The evidence shows conclusively, we say, that during these years Croats continued to be subjected to abuse, expulsion, and murder in the RSK. The police both participated in these crimes and failed to take any action against perpetrators. The evidence from this period is further support of the existence of the joint criminal enterprise and its common purpose to forcibly remove Croats from the Krajina. Moreover, it further supports particular counts in the indictment, including the persecutions count and the deportation and forcible transfer counts. Finally, we come to the Zagreb shelling counts; Counts 15 through 19 of the indictment.
