With respect to the shelling of Zagreb, the evidence shows, beyond any possible doubt, that Milan Martic ordered the shelling of Zagreb in a desperate and unsuccessful, I might say, attempt to stop Operation Flash in Western Slavonia. The evidence further establishes that Mr. Martic targeted Zagreb because it would have a maximum impact by causing maximum terror on the Croat side. He was not targeting military targets in Zagreb. That is obvious by his statements, statements of Mr. Celeketic, as well as by the simple fact that the Orkan rockets would not reasonably possibly be expected to cause significant damages to places like the Ministry of Defence, and certainly could not be expected that hitting such places with an Orkan rocket would have any effect whatsoever on Operation Flash. That is simple fantasy. But hitting Zagreb, the city, with all of its civilian inhabitants, now that could have an impact, or at least he thought. In the alternative, we say, even if it were found by this Trial Chamber that he was aiming at military targets, the weapons he used were necessarily indiscriminate and unlawful [Realtime transcript read in error "lawful"] under the circumstances. Now, with respect to Zagreb, the Defence makes three broad arguments in their brief. First, they make the extraordinary claim that it has not been proven that Mr. Martic ordered the shelling. Second, they make some points about reprisals, the law regarding reprisals, and claim also that the Croat side is to blame for having military targets in Zagreb. And then, third, they suggest that the Orkan rocket was an appropriate weapon to use. With respect to whether Mr. Martic ordered the shelling of Zagreb, the evidence is simply overwhelming that he did. He talked about doing it before it happened; and he repeatedly took credit, both in the media and in meetings, for doing it after it happened. Everybody, including Slobodan Milosevic, knew that Mr. Martic had ordered it. As the Trial Chamber itself pointed out at the beginning of this case, it's at page 221, Mr. Martic even admitted to ordering the bombing of Zagreb here in court, at the Tribunal, on the 26th of September, 2003. The Defence did not challenge any of the evidence put in by the Prosecution showing that he ordered the bombing and did not object when we said at the 98 bis stage of the case, and it's at page 5928 when we said it, that it was not really disputed that Mr. Martic ordered the shelling of Zagreb on May 2nd and May 3rd. The claim appears to have arisen for the first time during the testimony of Defence witness Patrice Barriot at the end of the case, and not on direct examination either, on cross-examination, when he was shown an open letter that he had written to Milan Martic in which he said that Mr. Martic had ordered the shelling of Zagreb. It's in evidence, but I don't have that exhibit number on hand. In court, Mr. Barriot claimed what he had written there, that Mr. Martic had ordered the shelling of Zagreb, he later learned or later came to believe was not true. When he was asked: Well, how did you learn that? First, he said: You have to place yourself in the context of the time, he said. That's at 10774. When he was pressed a little, he then said, well, that he had made an analysis of Mr. Martic's personality, that that's how he had come to believe it. That's at 10777. And then he said that -- and then he said that Mr. Martic had told him that he was willing to take responsibility for anything done by his subordinates. That's at 10778. The Prosecution submits that Mr. Barriot was simply trying to avoid in his testimony having to put any responsibility for anything on Mr. Martic. In fact, Mr. Barriot subsequently admitted in his testimony - it was actually in questions from the Prosecution after Your Honours' questions - that he had re-published the letter without correcting it, without changing what he had written about Mr. Martic ordering the bombing of Zagreb, in 2003, completely undermining his claim in court that he had come to learn or come to believe that Mr. Martic had, in fact, not ordered the shelling. None of the other evidence cited by the Defence undermines in any way the overwhelming evidence that Mr. Martic ordered the shelling. The Defence points to evidence showing that Mr. Celeketic ordered the shelling, but that is consistent with Mr. Martic ordering it. Obviously, the order would have had to go from Mr. Martic to Mr. Celeketic to the troops on the ground. The Defence also points to the fact that after the fall of Western Slavonia and the shelling of Zagreb, Mr. Celeketic was replaced, but the evidence is that he was replaced by Belgrade, not by Martic. Also, there is no evidence that he was disciplined or prosecuted for the shelling of Zagreb. Nothing cited by the Defence overcomes the evidence of repeated statements and the repeated understanding of witnesses that Mr. Martic ordered, himself, the shelling of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Before you go on, Mr. Whiting, I'd like to just deal with a matter on the transcript, which I think could be profound for posterity, and otherwise. If we look at page 52 of the transcript of the record at, or 51 -- sorry, 53, 1 and 2 and 25 of the previous page, it says, "even if it were found that this Trial Chamber" -- sorry, "even if it were found by this Trial Chamber that he was aiming at military targets, the weapons he used were necessarily indiscriminate and lawful under the circumstances." I think it should be "indiscriminate and unlawful."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, and I am grateful for your help there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It's a profound distinction. Sometimes I don't like to interrupt, but I think this one warrants an interruption; and could it therefore be corrected, because it is material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I fully agree. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry to interrupt and stop your flow at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. Actually, the timing was excellent because I think we've come to the time for our second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we break, was that what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I said it. It's what I have written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We wanted to get that on the record. That being the case, court adjourned, reconvene at half past 12.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First, before I continue, the exhibit that I was referring to Mr. Barriot's open letter, that's Exhibit Number 1011. Now, with respect to Zagreb, the second issue that the Defence raised in its brief was regarding reprisals and also whether Croatia could be held responsible for having purported military targets in Zagreb. Now, with respect to the issue of reprisals, I understand the Defence to be saying that they agree that reprisals against civilians are strictly prohibited, at least that's how I understand the beginning of paragraph 90 of their brief. However, just so this point is absolutely clear, there can be no question that reprisals against civilians or civilian objects are explicitly prohibited by paragraph 6 of Article 51 of Additional Protocol I, paragraph 1 of Article 52 of the same protocol, and Article 53. Moreover, I would refer the Trial Chamber to the Kordic appeals judgement, paragraphs 53 and 59; the Blaskic appeals judgement, paragraph 109; the Galic appeals judgement, paragraph 190 to 191; the Kupreskic trial judgement, paragraph it is 527 to 536; and the Rule 61 decision in this case, the Milan Martic case, which was rendered on the 8th of March, 1996, in particular paragraphs 15 to 17. Moreover, the law is clear and has been cited by this Trial Chamber in this case that it is irrelevant which side initiated the conflict, and I would refer the Trial Chamber to the Blaskic appeals judgement at paragraph 427, and it is irrelevant that the other side may have also committed crimes. Tu quoque, of course, is not a defence. It's clear that whatever was happening in Western Slavonia during Operation Flash, and the Defence devotes a number of pages to this in their final brief, it can no way justify the crimes that Milan Martic committed against Zagreb on May 2nd and May 3rd of 1995. Now, regarding the question of whether Croatia can be held responsible because purported military targets were located in Zagreb, and this is under Article 58 of Additional Protocol I. The Galic appeals judgement affirmed the Trial Chamber's conclusion in that case that a party's failure to abide by this obligation does not relieve the attacking side of its duty to abide by the principles of distinction and proportionality when launching an attack. That appears in paragraph 194 of the Galic appeals judgement. In this context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you want me to say it at this point, I was just going to ask whether in this case was there any military target shelled in Zagreb; and if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer to that is no. There was -- there was no military target hit. The evidence shows that there was no military target hit in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Is the contention from the Defence that that is the particular target that was being aimed at, that a particular target was being aimed at and not necessarily hit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. One of the arguments made by the Defence is that purported military targets, the Ministry of Defence, the presidential palace, the Ministry of the Interior, were what were being aimed at. Yes. None of those targets were hit. It is our contention that that was not the intent of the attack, that they were not being aimed at. Moreover, if they were being aimed at, an inappropriate weapon was used. The Defence also claims that the RSK provided warnings that it would shell Zagreb, and this is potentially relevant to the issue under Article 58 or possibly to the issue of reprisals, but here the Defence confuses vague threats with specific warnings. The fact that Milan Martic in November of 1994 threatened to shell Zagreb in a conversation with Ambassador Galbraith or even that the Croatian side thought that this might be something that the RSK would resort to does not amount to a warning, which would have to be specific as to time and place. Numerous witnesses, and this is set forth in our final brief, including Ambassador Galbraith, who was in Zagreb at the time of the shelling, testified that in fact there were no warnings before the attack. Finally, the Defence makes the argument that the Orkan was an appropriate weapon to use. First, they cite to Exhibit 94 which is a United Nations report which merely estimates that the precision of an Orkan rocket fired from a distance of 32 kilometres is 250 metres. It's not exactly clear what that means, 250 metres in every direction or -- it's not clear. In any event, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- Whether 250 metres is diameter or radius.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, it says nothing, it says 250 metres. And it explicitly says it's an estimate. This estimate cannot displace the expert report and evidence of Mr. Poje, which was based on the official firing tables for the Orkan rocket. And he estimated that when the Orkan was fired from a distance of 49 kilometres and the evidence in this case is that is how far the rockets were fired from on Zagreb, the Orkan fired from that distance could land approximately 1 kilometre in either direction from the intended target. That means 1 kilometre short, 1 kilometre too far, or 1 kilometre to the right and left. There is only a 50 percent chance that the rocket would land somewhere in a box around the target that is approximately 500 metres by 500 metres. In other words, 50 percent chance that it would land in that box, 500 metres by 500 metres, half a kilometre. Even that is an enormous margin of error and there it's just a 50 percent chance. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If fired from 32 kilometres, according to the estimate that you say the Defence relied upon, what would be the margin of error?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the report of Mr. Poje, he sets out -- he gives the margin for 20 kilometres, 40 kilometres, and 50 kilometres. I don't have the figures in front of me, but you would have to estimate the -- somewhere between the 20 and 40 to get the 32. I can say that it is higher than the 250 metres, though not enormously higher. I mean it -- but it's significant. I should say it is higher. I won't characterise it further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But what does the science say? Does it say the closer you are to the target, the less the margin of error?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. There's absolutely no doubt about that. The further away, the bigger the dispersion, the possible dispersion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, assuming the target as the Ministry of Defence, could you position the victim within the margin of error, the nearest victim? Do you understand my question? How does the margin of error relate to what actually happened, given the target of the Ministry of Defence in relation to the victims, the actual victims, on the ground when the bombs dropped. Were they within or without the margin of error?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can certainly say that some of the bombs fell within that margin of error, within the one kilometre in each direction margin of error. For example, the school, I think, is quite clearly within that one kilometre margin of error. I cannot say, standing here, whether the other locations fall within or without. My guess is that there is some that might also fall within, but I believe that there are others that fall outside of that margin of error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Following up on that point, what does the law say one's behaviour should be regulated -- how one's behaviour should be regulated if indeed there are civilian objects or civilians themselves within the margin of error area?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The law - and here is where I'm again speaking a bit on shorthand abbreviation. We've set it forth in our brief, so if I make any mistakes please rely on the brief - but the law says it's an issue of proportionality, that is, there has to be a calculation about the likelihood and degree of civilian casualties in relation to the value of the military target and the target being hit. And here -- and I guess I'm being told that it's in 468 of our brief we've set it out. Here we submit that when hitting an urban area, a densely populated urban area with civilians, that degree of area, that's enormous in Zagreb. One kilometre is basically anywhere in Zagreb. When you have a military target, the Ministry of Defence, the likelihood of very extensive and serious civilian casualties is almost a certainty actually. And Mr. Poje, in his expert report and in his testimony, said that based on -- he came to the conclusion that based on that analysis, based on the dispersion and the likelihood of civilian injuries, it was -- he came to the conclusion that it was an inappropriate weapon to use under those circumstances. A position which he re-affirmed again and again in his testimony under all the questions and scenarios posed to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you would say that even though, as I understand the Defence contention, the Ministry of Defence was the cell or the brain of the Croatian attack, that their backs were up against the wall given the onslaught and fierceness of the Croatian attack. That is their contention. I'm not saying that one necessarily agrees or does not agree at this point. And that under those circumstances the only way that they could protect themselves was to strike at the cell that was controlling the -- and directing the Croatian attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is our position, but I would like to address a number of the premises of the question. The first is that there is no evidence that the Croatian Ministry of Defence was the cell directing the attack. I'm not aware as I stand here that there is any such evidence. Secondly, it could not be reasonably expected that the Orkan rocket which is primarily an anti-personnel weapon designed to attack widespread armies would cause damage to the Ministry of Defence, a building we saw, a huge substantial building, that would cause the kind of damage to that building that could interrupt, even if it was the cell or the headquarters of the operation, that it would interrupt the operation being carried on. It would, at most, break a few windows of that building. Third, the evidence is that the operation actually was not in any way affected by the shelling of Zagreb. The operation only -- the Operation Flash only ended when the operation was successful, when it was completed. Given all the evidence, the reason that Zagreb was shelled was not to have any affect on those buildings, it was to cause a terrorist hit on Zagreb, to cause terror, and to try to force the Croatian government to respond because of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope this is the last time I'm asking you a question. You characterised the Orkan as an anti-personnel kind of weapon. Do we have evidence to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it is a completely inappropriate organ for purposes of structures like buildings?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Poje testified that it's well-known that the Orkan rocket is not designed to be a pin-point, hit a building type of weapon. It can of course cause damage to buildings, of course, but we can see what kind of damage it causes. It causes some broken windows and some damage to the roof. It's not going to bring down a building like the Ministry of Defence. It's not a pin-point weapon like that. It is a weapon that is designed primarily to attack over a wide terrain, an army, one example, an army that is spread out over a wide terrain. That is what the weapon is designed for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the kind of damage it causes would be the kind of damage we saw at the school, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Exactly. That's exactly right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, given the enormous margin of error of this weapon fired from the distance of 49 kilometres and the place that it was being fired on, an urban location, we say that there is just one word that describes that act: Criminal. The Defence further suggests, in footnote 277 of its brief, that Mr. Poje testified that the Orkan rocket was suitable for targets such as the Ministry of Defence and the presidential palace. However, go back, please, to the transcript that is cited and read it in its entirety. What in fact he was saying was that only in his view those were military targets. That is all that he was saying. He stated again and again and again that even assuming that those were military targets, that those were in Zagreb, that the Orkan rocket was an inappropriate weapon under the law, it was an inappropriate weapon to use to target those targets. The Defence further suggested that Milan Martic could not be held responsible for the choice of the Orkan rocket to attack, but this contention is simply false. First, Mr. Raseta, Prosecution witness, testified - and I would note that the Defence states in paragraph 150 of its brief that in their view, Mr. Raseta provided very reliable testimony - Mr. Raseta said that persons familiar with the Orkan knew that it was designed for targeting wider areas and not specific points. And he was certain, he was certain, that Mr. Martic knew about the shelling of Zagreb because Mr. Celeketic would have had to have told him. Let's remember that Mr. Celeketic spoke openly in the media before the attack on Zagreb, it's Exhibit 91, about his willingness to target civilians in cities. He said that in an interview. It's in our final brief, it's Exhibit 91. He spoke openly about that. There is no reason to believe that he would have hidden anything from his superior, Milan Martic. Of course, it's further evidence that Mr. Martic approved of the shelling that after the shelling on the 2nd of May, 1995, he did nothing to prevent the shelling the following day, the 3rd of May, 1995; and that was because he ordered the shelling on both of those days, supported it, and knew what was going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: He knew what was going to happen and he knew what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- to take you to his final conclusion. Did he or did he not punish Mr. Celeketic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The evidence is that he did not, Your Honour. All of the evidence is that he did not. There is no evidence that he punished Mr. Celeketic. Finally, the Defence contends that the use of the Orkan rocket was lawful because it was not as bad as another rocket that the RSK had, which was called the Luna rocket; and that they used the Orkan instead of the Luna rocket and, therefore, the Orkan rocket was lawful. And also they contend that these were the only weapons available to the RSK. The rules against targeting civilians in the law do not contain an exception, saying that you can do it if you -- if you do not -- if you do not possess an appropriate weapon, if it's your only weapon. That is just not the law, nor could it be the law. It also is not the law that you can use an inappropriate weapon if you choose not to use a weapon that would be even more inappropriate. That also is not the law, nor could it be the law. Mr. Poje testified that even if the Orkan rocket were the only weapon available to the RSK that could reach Zagreb, it was nonetheless an inappropriate weapon to use. That does not change his conclusion. In summary, in conclusion on the topic of Zagreb, it is our very strong contention that the evidence shows that civilians were the target in Zagreb. And we would ask for a finding of this Trial Chamber to that effect; that that was Mr. Martic's intent on the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1995, that's what he did, and we know what the result was. As I've said, there is the alternative finding, the alternative possibility that the Trial Chamber could find that if he did intend to hit military targets, that the rockets he used were clearly inappropriate weapons under the circumstances. Finally, we come to my last topic, and that is sentencing. The relevant law on this topic is set forth in our brief. The primary factor to be taken into account is the gravity of the offence. We've also set forth a number of aggravating factors that are supported by the law and which have been proven in this case beyond a reasonable doubt: Discriminatory intent for all crimes except for persecutions where discriminatory intent is an element of the crime, therefore, it cannot be considered an aggravating factor; the length of time the crimes were committed; the scale of the crimes, except for extermination where scale is arguably an element; premeditation; the status of the victims; the willing and enthusiastic participation of the accused; and the presence of civilian detainees. Now, in considering sentencing, should the Trial Chamber reach that point, we say that the Trial Chamber should also compare the culpability of Mr. Martic to that of Mr. Babic, who was sentenced by this Tribunal to a period of 13 years' imprisonment for his criminal conduct, to which he pled guilty. Now, bear in mind, of course, the Trial Chamber is not bound in any way, but this certainly should be considered. Bear in mind that Mr. Babic pled guilty to criminal conduct that occurred between the 1st of August, 1991, and the 15th of February, 1992, a more limited time than is charged against Mr. Martic. And, of course, Mr. Babic pled guilty and he cooperated with the Tribunal and testified in three trials, and therefore received a lower sentence than he otherwise might have. In considering the gravity of the offence and certain of the aggravating factors, considerable thought must be given to the many, many victims of the crimes in this case. We heard from just a fraction of the survivors, and we heard about lives and communities destroyed. Who can forget Jasna Denona from Bruska, who testified eloquently and bravely about when she was 15 years old, and her house and her village were attacked by members of the SAO Krajina police, and of being shot as she fled out the back of her house. Or of Marica Vukovic, who testified about her village of Poljanak being attacked on the 7th of November, 1991, of her husband and of her father being tied up and executed. Is it really possible for us to imagine the terror that she felt? Or Neven Segaric, who witnessed his grandparents being executed in Skabrnja. Or Stanko Erstic or Luka Brkic, who testified about the torture and the abuse, the humiliation and degradation that they suffered in the Knin old hospital and the JNA barracks in Knin. Remember the villages that were destroyed, the churches that were singled out in Croat villages. Witness after witness testified about leaving their villages and seeing everything burning and coming back years later to find everything destroyed. Vukovici was completely wiped out, virtually everyone there was murdered. Think about the execution that occurred in Nadin, in the destruction of that village. Think about Zagreb in May -- on May 2nd and May 3rd of 1995, beautiful spring/summer day. The seven people who were killed in those attacks, the hundreds who were injured, and no doubt the thousands who were terrified when the shells rained down on Zagreb on May 2nd and May 3rd. Remember just one example of Sanja Buntic who testified that she had escaped Sarajevo, the horrors of Sarajevo in October 1994 and came to Zagreb in order to have a normal life, only to be seriously injured when Zagreb was shelled. Remember, too, that there are all of the obvious ways that victims' lives are destroyed, but there are also many ways that we might not think about right away. Remember Sanja Risovic? She was at the children's hospital at Klaiceva Street on the 3rd of May, 1995, with her 4-month-old infant when the shells hit. She testified about her injuries and she testified about how those injuries affected her life. I just want to play a little clip from her testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "Q. Have the injuries had any impact on your ability to take care of your young daughter? "A. Of course they have. My child was 4 months old at the time. When I decided to have the child, I wanted to be her mother. I wanted to extend all my love and tenderness to her, to be with her. And at one point, I was no longer able to be with her; and when I was eventually discharged, I couldn't carry my child. I couldn't change her diapers because for a long time I could not move my right hand. I could not feed my baby. "At the end of the day, my motherhood, a lot of it, a good part of my motherhood was spent at various hospitals in rehabilitation. And at one point, my child was asked at the kindergarten where her mother was. He said: 'My mother lives at home in a green building and in a hotel.' The green building was the hospital and a hotel was the spa. I was shocked. I didn't understand how she could say something like that, but it only made sense. Because if the -- her mother didn't live with her, she perceived the places where I was as my home. "I spent very little time with her, unfortunately, and all my life I will regret the fact that I did not spend more time with my baby. Every mother wants to spend as much time with their child as they possibly can, to nurture and to look after their baby. And in my life, there came a time when I could not look after my child in any way."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, all of the crimes in this case, individually and together, were extraordinarily grave and horrific. The criminal conduct lasted for years and years. It affected men, women, the elderly, children. The Prosecution, therefore, recommends that for the crimes in this case, individually and together - and I emphasise individually and together - the accused, Milan Martic, should be sentenced to a term of imprisonment of life in prison. In closing, I will say only this: Milan Martic came to the Tribunal and entered a plea of not guilty to the charges against him, as was his right under the Statute and the Rules. He asked for a trial, which was also his right, at which he has been and continues to be presumed innocent and can only be found guilty if the charges against him are proven beyond a reasonable doubt, a heavy burden for the Prosecution. He has now had that trial, Your Honours. The witnesses have come and testified in front of him, often requiring extraordinary bravery. They've been questioned, they have been cross-examined, and all of the exhibits have been placed before you. We submit, Your Honours, that now the time has come for Mr. Martic to be held responsible for the crimes that he has committed and to be found guilty of those crimes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I must pose this question to you, bearing in mind that you ended by asking for life imprisonment. So if you will permit me, as I understand it, this sentence would be at the top end of sentencing -- of the sentencing bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And as I understand it, reserved for certain categories and by their nature certain very -- going to a certain level of heinousness. Now, my recollection is that there has been a rapid development of sentencing in domestic international spheres, that is acknowledged internationally to tend to place more emphasis on the element of reform and restoration of the particular convict to his society to make a meaningful contribution. Now, given that the circumstances, the subject matter of the charges, if a conviction does result, because it might not, given that they result out of conflict, international conflict between ethnic groups, would you discount the issue of reform in war crimes and in this sphere, and would you discount the acknowledged development of the law of sentencing to accommodate a more sensitive approach to the accused, even given the circumstances that serious crimes have been committed? And would you still in those circumstances ask for a life imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll answer your last question first, Your Honour. The answer to your last question is going to be: Yes. But let me address your specific questions as thoroughly as I can. The first is that Your Honour -- Your Honour, you indicated that it is of course the sentence at the very top end. It is reserved for the most serious crimes. Of course, just last month, in the Galic case, the Appeals Chamber imposed a sentence of life imprisonment for the crimes -- the conviction in that case. And in our view, the crimes in this case, even certain of the crimes individually, are as or more serious than the crimes in that case. So there's certainly precedent in this Tribunal for such a sentence to be imposed. And there are particular -- there are particular circumstances in this case that really bring it up, which are in my view the long-term nature of the crimes. The fact that these crimes went on from 1991 until 1995 all over the Krajina again and again and again. That is just one of the aggravating circumstances but there are others. And taken all together, the circumstances of this case really stand out and warrant the highest possible sentence. The second point with respect to what Your Honour describes as the acknowledged development of the law of sentencing, I'm not sure I would agree with Your Honour about that. I think it depends very much on what jurisdictions you're talking about in -- I think in certain jurisdictions, the -- there are a series of questions about the ability to reform serious criminals, particularly ones that have committed crimes like these. And in my view, no matter what jurisdiction you're talking about, whether it -- whether it is moving in that direction or not, the kinds of crimes that we're talking about here, where, by the way, there has been no remorse whatsoever, no indication that reform is even possible, rather, what I would suggest is we've seen justification. But even in jurisdictions where reform might be on the rise in sentencing, I would say that with this kind of a case the gravity of the offences, the seriousness of them would predominate and this would not be a case where reform would rise up as a predominant consideration. And to take this one step further, Your Honour, I would hazard if this case if there were convictions on these kinds of crimes in any national jurisdiction in the world that a life sentence would be appropriate. I mean, certainly in the country I come from and in many other countries, maybe not -- maybe I can't say every country. But for these kinds of crimes, the most serious crimes on earth, a life sentence -- there is really no other sentence. It is the sentence -- it is the appropriate sentence in national jurisdictions and it's the appropriate sentence here. And I say that, and I emphasise that that is true in our view even if he was not convicted of all the crimes in the indictment, that is why I said individually and separately -- I mean individually and together. Now, I'm not sure if I eve answered all of your questions but I tried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I want to thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we ask Mr. Milovancevic to stand up, there's just one little point I'd like to raise. This morning the Chamber indicated that there was an outstanding housekeeping issue to be dealt with, and that housekeeping issue was not dealt with to finality. It was overtaken by other issues that arose. May I at this stage ask then that based on the fact that both the Prosecution and the Defence had no objection to the admission into evidence of the maps that were provided by the Bench, and indeed the Prosecution has used one of them in its argument this afternoon, that those maps be then be now admitted into evidence and be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the maps become Exhibit Number 1044.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, given the time and given the fact that the closing arguments of the Prosecution just concluded and they were quite long and not easy to follow, we ask that we be allowed to begin with our closing arguments tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I beg your pardon. You can't do anything in those 30 minutes, Mr. Milovancevic? And if you can't and you want us to start tomorrow, you must then guarantee us that you will finish tomorrow and not go into -- because the next day is for reply by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is hard for me to guarantee that I will conclude tomorrow, but I will do my best to conclude tomorrow. I can't be positive and tell you that it is 100 percent certain that I will. We heard the closing arguments of the Prosecution today, and it has certain weight and certain effect. And we believe that under the circumstances we should begin tomorrow. This is our request, our kind request. All I can say is that in our view I can guarantee you that everything will be concluded on Friday, including the reply. All of that should be concluded by the end of business on Friday, so I don't think that we will go into next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear that and I would have been sympathetic to your request. But without guaranteeing that you'll finish tomorrow, I'm afraid that I will have to ask you to start. Mr. Milovancevic, 30 minutes is a long enough time. We can break off at some point. Start with your own arguments and you can deal with the Prosecution's argument, if that's what you want to study overnight and rebut.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it is the decision of the Trial Chamber that the Defence is to begin its closing arguments today, the Defence will comply. We have no other choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main position of the Defence is that the Prosecution failed to prove the allegations from the indictment, all of them. The indictment constitutes a fiction. It was not supported by the evidence adduced during trial. It is our position that this was a mere construction which was accomplished in the following way: Namely, a portion of territory and a certain period of time were taken out of context of the territory, time, and real events. They applied a selective approach to the events in the territory of Yugoslavia, thereby modelling this indictment. It is unusual, Your Honours, that in paragraph 3 of their final brief, which is their final submission, the Prosecution says that this case is not about who is to blame for the disintegration of Yugoslavia. They say that this case is not about who started the war. They also say that it is not about whether the war could have been avoided; that it is not about events that occurred in World War II; that this case is not about the role of the international community in the events in Yugoslavia. They also say that this case is not about whether the Republic of Croatia acted legally or illegally under the laws of Yugoslavia; and that it is also not about the motives of the alleged members of the joint criminal enterprise; and that this case is not about whether Croat forces themselves committed crimes before, during, or after the war. It is illogical for the Prosecution to say this because, first of all, this court was established in order to try for the most grave violations of the international law in the territory of the former Yugoslavia; thus, this court is authorised to try cases concerning the events in the former Yugoslavia. Second, the Prosecutor, by way of this paragraph 3, denies the right of the Defence to deal with all of these questions -- dealing with all of these questions themselves. The Prosecution uses these allegations in order to create an indictment and to prove the alleged guilt of Mr. Martic. They say that this case is not about the blame for the disintegration of Yugoslavia, and they go on to quote the reports of the Badinter Commission which dealt precisely with this issue. The Prosecution says that this case is not about who started the war, and they go on to claim that it was Mr. Martic who did that; then they say that this case is not about whether the war could have been avoided. And at the same time, they kept putting to the Trial Chamber the statement given by Mr. Tudjman on the 24th of May, 1992, who said that there would have been no war had Croatia given up on its independence; then they go on to say that this case is not about the role of international community. However, we spent hours and hours and tens of thousands of dollars in order to review the provisions of Vance Plan, plan Z-4, the reports to the Security Council, a whole myriad of Security Council Resolutions, and these were all issues dealt with by the Prosecution, primarily by the Prosecution, in their attempt to prove the guilt of Mr. Martic; then they go on to say that this case is not about the motives of those who allegedly participated in joint criminal enterprise. In my working experience, I never heard of any perpetrator acting without a motive. I think that the Prosecution will have to deal with these issues, and essentially they did. The only motive for these alleged or real crimes that the Prosecution spoke of and accused Mr. Martic of, so the only motive is chauvinism, intolerance, ruthlessness in relation to members of a certain religion or ethnic group: Muslims and Croats in their view. Many of the witnesses of the Prosecution confirmed, including, for example, Witness MM-78, who is somebody who went to school with Mr. Martic. So many of the witnesses claim that they never observed any traces of hatred or any kind of intolerance in him against members of Croatian community. And he was not the only witness to state something of this nature. The Prosecution say that this is not a case dealing with crimes committed by Croats allegedly before, during, or after the war; however, in their indictment, the Prosecution actually conceal Croatian crimes and their own responsibility for failure to prosecute for these crimes. The indictment against Mr. Martic was issued 50 days after the shelling of Zagreb. The attack against the zone under the protection of the United Nations and the massacre of civilians referred to in the report of the United Nations, reports of UNPROFOR and UNCIVPOL, and also something that was mentioned in evidence of Croatian colonel, Colonel Gruic. All of this data show that for over ten years the Prosecution had in their hands evidence about the most brutal crimes committed in Western Slavonia at the time when Mr. Martic allegedly took his revenge against Zagreb. When we tried to establish the connection between these crimes and the action taken against Zagreb, against civilian targets in Zagreb, we were told that this was tu quoque defence. Your Honours, this is not tu quoque defence. This is the Defence defending, or rather, concealing the blame of the Prosecution for their failure not to prosecute for these grave crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. You asked us why we did not raise this issue with the Prosecution. It is not up to the Defence to prosecute for these crimes. No, it is up to the Prosecution to prosecute for these crimes. And the Prosecution not only failed to prosecute for this, but they twisted the picture about what happened in Western Slavonia. By doing so, they protected Croatian leadership and Croatian state for their blame of these crimes. They also shifted their own blame were, their own responsibility for this failure. And by doing so, they put Mr. Martic in a situation where they think that it is only life sentence that is an appropriate sentence for his alleged deeds. These are just some introductory remarks relative to paragraph 3 of the final brief. What is important for the Trial Chamber here is this: The evidence on file which was presented through various witnesses and written evidence that was offered by the Prosecution show that in the territory of the European state of Yugoslavia there was an armed rebellion; that there was an armed rebellion that was organised, implemented, and carried out by the authorities of the new independent state of Croatia headed by Mr. Tudjman. During their case, the Prosecution called witness Imre Agotic, the former colonel of JNA. Through him the Prosecution tried to prove to the Trial Chamber something that is incontestable and that was proven by Defence witnesses, and that arises from Exhibit 402. And this is that it is a correct statement by Antun Tus, the colonel of the Yugoslav army. The Yugoslav army towards the end of 1991 had 200.000 completely armed men; that they had 230 tanks, the tanks that had been captured from the JNA, and he was referring to the Croatian army; that it had over 400 heavy artillery pieces; that it had anti-aircraft defence and coast artillery. In other words, that it was completely armed, an army of force that at the time, as was testified by Colonel Peric, was ten times stronger than the armed members of the JNA that were deployed in the territory of Croatia at the time. What about the fact that the Prosecutor proved in this case through Colonel Agotic in 1991, in November, there were 24 brigades; and towards the end of 1991 there was 63 brigades of the Croatian army, bearing in mind that in the territory of a sovereign state that had its own armed force, which at the time was the JNA that represented the legitimate armed force of the existing state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. I believe your pace is a little bit too quick. I hear the interpreter struggling, and I myself would like to have you slow down just a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for your warning, and I would like you to keep doing that again because I don't do it deliberately. In a territory of a sovereign state, when illegal armed forces appear with a view to breaking that country apart, to defeat the federal army, and with the ultimate goal of creating an independent state of Croatia that Mr. Tudjman was referring to, then this is an armed rebellion and nothing else. This is not just the position of the Defence, this is also an issue that has been answered explicitly by Mr. Maksic, colonel of the JNA, a person who graduated from highest military schools. He said that there were massive attacks against the JNA that lasted from mid-1991 towards the end of 1992. It was not only Mr. Maksic who said that, it was also a Prosecution witness, expert Theunens who said that. He appeared on the Prosecution side as a military expert. When the question was put to him: What was the meaning of the invitation by Mr. Tudjman on 5th of May, 1991, for the barracks of the JNA to be blocked, and also what was the meaning of the attacks against the JNA that ensued, and what was the meaning of the 14 cease-fires that took place during the fighting and that were in favour of the Croatian armed forces, the expert Theunens answered: This was an armed rebellion. In Defence's view, he actually omitted to say it was an armed rebellion. He just said it was a rebellion, but in the Defence's view he omitted the word armed rebellion deliberately. General Borislav Djukic also spoke about an armed rebellion. He is a person who also completed highest military schools and who described his participation in what he later on described as an armed rebellion. Colonel Peric, another Defence witness, also spoke about this armed rebellion and he characterised it as such. And how did it look like, what were its characteristics is something that we will deal with tomorrow because we have not prepared the film that will help us to do that. But we are going to do it tomorrow, Your Honours. When the Prosecution brought their witness, Colonel -- the former colonel of JNA Agotic into this courtroom, and when they introduced his statement according to Rule 92 bis into this case, and when this witness confirmed that the Croatian army had 63 heavily armed brigades which were used for operations in the territory of the Republic of Croatia in the year 1991, and when he said that in July 1991 he left the and that in August 1991 he was appointed by President Tudjman as the Chief of Staff of the ZNG, the Croatian armed forces, which at the time was an illegal armed formation, and that he remained in that position until 21 September 1991, when the staff of the Croatian army was established, then Colonel Agotic confirmed that in the territory of the sovereign European territory of Yugoslavia, illegal rebellious armed forces of the Republic of Croatia were active, and at the time the Republic of Croatia was still an active member of the Yugoslav federation. Bearing in mind the fact that this witness informed us that Mr. Tudjman appointed him as a special envoy in negotiations, i.e., as an authorised negotiator according to this witness's words with the JNA when it came to the withdrawal of the JNA from Croatia, and when this witness said that the negotiations started on the 8th of October, 1991, and lasted until the end of 1991, when the JNA finally withdrew from Croatia, then this is another proof by the Prosecution that has to be trusted. There are some pieces of evidence that shouldn't be trusted, and we will tell you why. But the previous one that I've just described should be trusted completely. The witness Imre Agotic, the Prosecution witness I've just mentioned, has also confirmed the veracity of Exhibit 402, which is the statement by General Anton Tus, another former officer of the JNA. He was a general. He was the commander of the JNA air force. In 1991, in Zagreb, Croatia captured 38.000 rifles and 20 million bullets, according to this general. A lot of those were sent to the so-called crisis areas. The arms and bullets were indeed sent to the crisis areas, which was confirmed by Marko Vukovic and Vlado Vukovic from Saborsko who were Prosecution witnesses. They were policemen from Saborsko, and they spoke about two occasions. The first one on the 24th of September and another occasion in October when a unit with over a hundred men arrived in the area, bringing ammunition and all the other pieces of equipment in 9 to 11 trucks. This was also confirmed by a Defence witness, Medakovic, who also hails from that same area. Another Prosecution witness, that is Imre Agotic, a Prosecution witness, confirmed General Tus's statement according to which not only there was a Croatian army with 200.000 heavily armed men, but also that plans had already been put in place to liberate Knin from various directions. But they were interrupted by the adoption of the Vance Plan and by the arrival of UNPROFOR. And, finally, witness Agotic confirmed that as the then-high Croatian official, the Chief of Staff of the ZNG and then authorised Tudjman's envoy negotiations with the JNA, that he was familiar with what was going on in Saborsko in November 1991, because the representatives of the local community had called him very often, asking for assistance that would alleviate tensions in Saborsko and that would help Saborsko to arm themselves and to defend themselves. In other words, the representative of the local community of Saborsko asked for arms to defend themselves. We will talk about that later. However, Colonel Agotic explained in his testimony that in Saborsko there was a unit of the Croatian police and that people organised themselves there. Just like all the other villages up to Setis Poljana, which is south-east towards Saborsko towards Petroski Eozella. We are talking about the Exhibit 389 and page 23.314. In other words, all the villages southeast of Saborsko, Setis Poljana up to Petris Eozella, were armed and they had Croatian armed forces stationed there. And, finally, the Prosecution proved another very important thing through this witness. The colonel did negotiate with the JNA, and he stayed in the JNA up to July 1992. And according to the information that arrived from Belgrade, the federal secretariat, through its political unit, to all the units of the JNA gave a task to preserve Yugoslavia at all costs. All the members of the JNA were informed about that. They were familiar with that order. In other words, a member of the rebel sort, a deserter, and a traitor, a person you who decided to forget the oath he had taken to his army and went to the enemy side, he said the goal of the JNA was to preserve Yugoslavia at any cost. Since we're drawing to an end of today's day, the question imposes itself: What does it mean to preserve a country at any cost? A country is preserved at any cost only when it is attacked at any cost. In other words, in only one small portion of the Yugoslav territory, there were 200.000 irregular military troops organised, well-equipped, well-supplied, and led into an armed rebellion, which they implemented through 63 independent brigades. This is what the Prosecution proved. In that, they organised this armed rebellion in every single corner where their population by delivering arms to them. This is confirmed by Imre Agotic. The head of the defence of Skabrnja also confirmed that by saying there was a battalion in Skabrnja. Also, it was confirmed that one-third of the territory of the SDA radar municipality was under control of the Croatian army. This was said by Milincic, a Prosecution witness. And Brkic, another Prosecution witness, told us at the time in Saborsko they had boots, uniforms of the east German army. They had belt, automatic rifles, and other weapons in Saborsko. We'll go into greater detail of all the evidence to prove that such units existed in Kijevo; that in Vrpolje and in Potkonje there were people who had received illegal weapons by the HDZ and it was only the Croatian population that received such weapons; and that in a number of other places, Kosta, Bacin, and Dubica there are members of the HDZ who had been illegally armed and led by the HDZ, the ZNG, and the new Croatian MUP. The Prosecution has proved through their witnesses that this was an organised, armed rebellion. The international law has its provisions about an armed rebellion and about the authorities of a country in which an armed rebellion is being staged and carried out. And this is something we will go into tomorrow. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We've come to the end of the session for today. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in the same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
